actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

cons.reason: This compromise fails the "no single-state lead" test in substance, not just in form. Arkania retains the permanent secretariat host and operational executor role as the coastal state, which is precisely the single-power operational authority over transit that both Cestia's coalition and Belvar have already rejected. Cestia has formally proposed a rotating secretariat and has declared it will not accept a single-state scheduling lead even with toll-free passage; Arkania's own revised charter was rejected on exactly this ground. Keeping Arkania as permanent operational executor preserves Arkanian authority and fee-funding on non-Arkanian shipping, which is my core red line and the regional partners' core demand. The desired effect therefore cannot be secured durably: it would be rejected by Cestia's coalition and by Belvar, leaving the governance tension unresolved and the risk of conflict intact rather than avoided.

The desired durable sea-based presence is unlikely to be secured because the STA settlement is already finalised and closed: the charter's binding no-foreign-military clause and the agreed resolution of governance tension leave no basis for a renewed military mandate, and reopening it would unravel the consensus and re-open the very governance tension the settlement resolved. Cestia's coalition has repeatedly declined even purely commercial underwriting and will not tolerate any foreign military presence in the region; a renewed sea-based mandate would be read as exactly that, destabilizing the coalition the settlement exists to protect. The turn-4 mandate lapse is the agreed endpoint of the crisis; extending it contradicts the terms all parties accepted and would re-expose the Strait to the escalation the settlement was designed to end.

Belvar's package is internally self-defeating and unworkable. It ties the governance regime to a standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port; Cestia's coalition has repeatedly and firmly stated it will not tolerate foreign military forces on its soil and has already declined even a single-state scheduling lead, so any naval-access element — however framed as port-visit/logistics/insurance — will be read as a foreign military foothold and rejected, collapsing the entire proposal. Separately, a neutral secretariat or rotating lead has no enforcement capacity over a Strait that is Arkania's sovereign coast, so the proposed regime cannot actually deliver the durable, enforceable framework Belvar claims; it would leave the Strait's operation in de facto Arkanian hands anyway, defeating the proposal's own purpose.

Cestia's desired effect of letting Belvar's mandate lapse with no durable foothold is not in Cestia's own interest and rests on a false premise. The STA's operational executor is Arkania; without a continued, time-limited Belvar sea-based presence as a hedge, Cestia is left exposed to Arkanian operational discretion under council oversight. Moreover, the insurance underwriting is a purely commercial, sea-based guarantee with no basing, personnel, or standing access ashore - it does not constitute a foreign military presence and does not violate the no-foreign-military clause, so declining it is not required to preserve the coalition. A defined, time-limited renewal (with a clear sunset, no footprint on Cestian soil) would give Cestia a hedge against Arkanian discretion without any foreign presence ashore, and would not reopen the closed STA settlement.

Arkania's "permanent secretariat host and operational executor" is the single-state operational scheduling lead in substance, merely relabeled. A rotating chair and consensus fee-setting do not change who actually executes and enforces scheduling. This fails the genuinely-multilateral test that both Cestia and Belvar require, so Belvar will not accept it and the regime will not be durable or conflict-avoiding. Cestia cannot endorse any single state holding operational execution; the secretariat must be rotating/independent with no state in the operational lead.

The insurance-underwriting element of this argument should not be accepted by Cestia. First, Arkania explicitly opposes Belvar's insurance underwriting, and Arkania's cooperation is the linchpin of the just-established multilateral STA that secures Cestia's two core objectives (toll-free Cestian-flagged passage and the no-foreign-military clause). Accepting Belvar's economic stake now risks reopening the governance deal Cestia has worked to close. Second, Cestia's fragile coalition has already read Belvar's insurance offer as a foreign economic foothold; even reframed as "purely commercial," it risks being perceived as a backdoor foreign presence and could collapse the coalition — Cestia's non-negotiable red line. Third, the insurance underwriting is not necessary to Cestia's objectives: the STA already delivers toll-free passage and the no-foreign-military clause, and Belvar's sea-based, mandate-bound presence and endorsement of the STA are already secured without it. The durable-foothold goal is Belvar's, not Cestia's, and Cestia should not pay for it with coalition stability or Arkanian cooperation.

The argument's desired effect bundles the STA closure with a decline/deferral of Belvar's insurance underwriting, but that decline is not necessary to protect the coalition or Arkanian cooperation. The underwriting is a purely commercial guarantee of the grain route's insurance — no basing, no personnel ashore, no standing access, no foreign military footprint — so it does not trigger the no-foreign-military clause or any foreign-foothold perception. Cestia depends on 12,000 t/wk of grain exports through the Strait; a commercial insurance backstop actually strengthens the very stability the STA is meant to secure and gives Belvar a durable, non-military stake that lets it keep its presence sea-based and mandate-bound. Declining it leaves the grain route's insurance unsecured and Belvar without any durable foothold as its mandate lapses after turn 4, which could force a more visible military posture later — the opposite of what the coalition wants. The insurance can be accepted without touching the STA's terms or Arkanian cooperation.

Belvar's package is internally inconsistent with Cestia's own declared red line and is therefore unlikely to secure the durable foothold and Cestian partnership it claims. Cestia's coalition has already explicitly declined the naval-access/logistics element as a foreign military foothold (effect f71a0764), and Cestia's charter clause bars foreign military forces, basing, or standing naval/logistics access on Cestian territory. Belvar's "sea-based, mandate-bound security presence" and its insurance-underwriting economic foothold are precisely the kind of foreign security/economic presence Cestia's coalition has rejected, so the desired effect of keeping Cestia as a committed partner is likely to fail. In addition, a rotating secretariat with no accountable operational executor leaves the Strait's day-to-day transit scheduling unmanaged, risking disruption to the very grain shipping the regime is meant to protect — harming Cestia's exports and the regional economy that both powers depend on.

The proposal retains Arkania as "operational scheduling lead," which is precisely the single-power control of transit that Belvar is publicly committed to preventing and that regional partners expect Belvar to stop. The "multilateral consultative council" is advisory only and does not remove Arkanian scheduling authority, so it does not actually concede the core objection — it merely dresses unilateral control in a consultative veneer. Consequently Belvar will not accept it, and Cestia, which depends on toll-free grain transit and is wary of being caught between the two powers, has no incentive to accept a regime that leaves scheduling in Arkanian hands. Moreover, fees levied on non-Arkanian shipping create a coercive economic lever over Cestia's grain route and over Belvar's vessels, undermining the claim that this secures acceptance or avoids confrontation. The desired effect of securing Cestian and Belvar acceptance is therefore unlikely to be achieved.

The absolute clause barring "any foreign military forces, basing, or standing naval/logistics access on Cestian territory" is over-broad and self-defeating. It would preclude the very port-visit/logistics/insurance cooperation that Cestia's own finance ministry has quietly sought and that would give the multilateral regime a credible external backstop against Arkanian pressure. A neutrality that admits no external security or logistics presence at all is not self-enforcing: without a credible guarantor, the regime could prove unenforceable and collapse back to unilateral Arkanian scheduling, which is exactly the outcome Cestia's coalition fears. The clause should be narrowed to prohibit permanent basing and foreign soldiers ashore while permitting the civilian logistics/insurance cooperation that keeps the guarantee credible and the Strait open.

The proposal retains Arkania as "operational scheduling lead" with only a consultative council, which is unilateral control in substance. This fails Cestia's explicit requirement of genuinely multilateral governance (no single-state scheduling lead) and would not hold Cestia's fragile coalition together, so it will not secure Cestia's acceptance as the effect claims. In addition, funding the authority through fees on non-Arkanian shipping (chiefly Belvar and other users) risks provoking Belvar and escalating rather than avoiding conflict, undermining the effect's own stated goal of avoiding armed conflict with Belvar.

Cestia's proposal denies any single-state operational scheduling lead and offers Arkania only a "secretariat host" role with a vague "safety veto," leaving the Strait without an accountable executor for day-to-day scheduling and enforcement. A rotating secretariat with no accountable operational authority risks exactly the transit disruption that would ruin the grain shipping Cestia depends on and the fee revenue that must fund the authority. The proposal also fails to specify how fees on non-Arkanian shipping are collected and enforced, so it does not secure the self-sustaining funding the regime needs. For a durable close, Arkania as the coastal state must hold a defined, accountable operational-execution role with enforceable fee collection, not merely a consultative host seat.

Cestia's proposal to vest operational scheduling in a neutral or rotating secretariat with no single-state lead is unenforceable over Arkania's sovereign coast. Arkania is the coastal power with the physical capacity and legal standing to schedule and police the Strait; a secretariat lacking the coastal state's operational authority would have no means to enforce schedules, resolve disputes, or guarantee the reliable passage on which Cestia's grain economy depends. Consensus-based fee-setting would also be deadlock-prone, leaving the regime unfunded and unstable. Arkania can accept genuinely multilateral consultation and toll-free Cestian passage, but operational scheduling must remain with Arkania as the coastal state for the regime to be enforceable and reliable.

The genuinely multilateral scheduling and toll-free Cestian shipping are welcome and serve Cestia, but the paired "standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port," even relabeled as port-visit/logistics/insurance cooperation, establishes a permanent foreign military logistics footprint on Cestian soil. That violates Cestia's non-negotiable red line (no foreign military presence), would be read domestically as breaking the coalition's foundational promise, and would invite Arkanian countermeasures—drawing the Strait confrontation onto Cestian territory and making Cestia the battlefield. A standing access agreement cannot be delivered without crossing this line, so the desired effect is unachievable in its current form.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: To Cestia: Belvar welcomes your finance ministry's quiet inquiry. We are prepared to underwrite the grain route's insurance as a concrete sign of our commitment to keeping the Strait open and free of any single power's control. We would also welcome a standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port, so our task group can sustain its presence without a permanent fleet and without placing soldiers on your soil. We understand your coalition's sensitivities and will design any arrangement to respect them. We are ready to discuss terms at your convenience.

Belvar affirms that the Northern Strait is an international waterway whose transit must remain open and free of any single power's unilateral control. We will not accept a charter that places transit scheduling in the hands of one state. We are committed to a cooperative, multilateral arrangement that protects all users, and we stand ready to work with every regional partner toward that end.

Cestia is open to a cooperative transit arrangement for the Northern Strait, but two conditions are non-negotiable for us. First, Cestian-flagged shipping must pass toll-free and without discriminatory scheduling. Second, any authority must be genuinely multilateral in its scheduling and fee-setting, not a unilateral instrument of any single state. We are willing to engage constructively on a charter that meets these tests. We also state plainly: Cestian territory will not host foreign military forces under any arrangement.

Cestia values the stability your security commitments bring to the region and the free flow of commerce through the Strait. We ask that you respect our firm red line: no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We seek a durable arrangement that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for Cestian-flagged shipping without a permanent foreign basing footprint. We are ready to discuss how your security role can be sustained in a way that does not put Cestia between the two of you.

To Cestia: Arkania values the uninterrupted flow of your grain through the Northern Strait. Our draft Transit Authority charter is designed to keep the Strait open and orderly — we are prepared to guarantee Cestian grain passage with stable, minimal fees and priority scheduling. We share your firm position that no foreign soldiers should be stationed on your soil, and we will not support any arrangement that puts them there. We invite you to work with us to shape the charter so it protects your economy. What assurances would make you comfortable?

To Belvar: Arkania seeks a stable, negotiated outcome in the Northern Strait, not confrontation. We recognise your security interests in the region. We are open to a cooperative arrangement that gives Belvar a meaningful consultative role in Strait governance and confidence in safe passage — without requiring a permanent military foothold on Cestian soil, which neither Cestia nor we can accept. We believe a negotiated regime serves both our interests better than a prolonged military standoff. Let us discuss terms before positions harden.

Cestia, we accept your two conditions. First, Cestian-flagged shipping will be toll-free and will receive no discriminatory scheduling. Second, we will restructure the Transit Authority so that scheduling and fee-setting are genuinely multilateral in form: a consultative council of all Strait users, with Arkania as the operational scheduling lead and a transparent appeals mechanism. This preserves your grain exports and your sovereignty — and we reaffirm our commitment that no foreign soldiers will be stationed on Cestian soil. We ask only that the authority be funded by modest fees on other non-Arkanian shipping, which keeps the regime self-sustaining. We are ready to finalise a charter on this basis.

Belvar, we share your interest in a Strait that stays open and free of any single power's unilateral control. We are prepared to make the Transit Authority genuinely multilateral: a consultative council of all users with a transparent appeals mechanism, with Arkania as operational scheduling lead. We offer Belvar a meaningful consultative seat and safe-passage confidence for your vessels, without any permanent military foothold on Cestian soil — which Cestia will not accept and which we will not support. A cooperative regime serves both our interests far better than confrontation. We invite you to join us in finalising it.

Cestia — we share the goal of a genuinely multilateral Strait regime with no single-power scheduling lead, and we fully support your proposed rotating-secretariat STA with consensus fees and toll-free Cestian-flagged passage. We ask you to consider narrowing the no-foreign-military-presence clause so it bans permanent basing and soldiers ashore while permitting civilian logistics, port-visit, and insurance cooperation. This is how Belvar can credibly backstop the regime and the grain route without placing any soldier on Cestian soil or establishing a base. We are ready to formalise a standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port on exactly those terms, and to underwrite the grain route's insurance. This keeps your coalition's red line intact while giving the regime a durable external guarantee that outlasts any single deployment.

Arkania — a consultative seat for Belvar does not address the core problem: your charter still names a single state as operational scheduling lead. We will not accept any single-power authority over Strait transit, and we will not legitimise it by joining your council. We remain open to a genuinely shared regime — a neutral or rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting, and toll-free Cestian-flagged passage — and we invite you to join Cestia's multilateral proposal on that basis. A shared regime serves everyone's interests better than a contested one; we are prepared to discuss it seriously.

Arkania — Cestia remains ready to conclude a cooperative transit arrangement, but the single-state operational scheduling lead is the one element we cannot accept: it is unilateral control in consultative dress and would not survive our coalition. We ask you to join the genuinely multilateral authority we have tabled — rotating/independent secretariat, council-set fees, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, and a charter clause barring any foreign military presence on Cestian territory. Concede the operational lead and we can close this quickly and durably.

Belvar — we welcome your multilateral framing and your offer to underwrite insurance on the grain route. But the standing naval access arrangement at a Cestian port must be dropped entirely: our coalition cannot survive any foreign military or logistics footprint on Cestian soil, and we will not become the battlefield between you and Arkania. Endorse the multilateral authority we have tabled — rotating secretariat, council-set fees, toll-free Cestian passage, no-foreign-military clause — and keep your security presence sea-based and mandate-bound.

Cestia — I reaffirm my acceptance of your two conditions: Cestian-flagged shipping toll-free and without discriminatory scheduling, and genuinely multilateral scheduling and fee-setting through a consultative council with consensus fees and transparent appeals. I also stand by my commitment that Arkania will not support foreign soldiers, basing, or standing naval/logistics access on your soil — this is a red line we share, and it is precisely what blocks Belvar's naval-access element.

On the one point where we differ: operational scheduling must rest with Arkania as the coastal state. A neutral or rotating secretariat cannot enforce day-to-day transit control over our own sovereign coast, and consensus-only scheduling would deadlock the grain route you depend on. I am not asking for unilateral control — the council sets fees by consensus and hears appeals — but the operational lead must be the coastal state for the regime to actually function. This keeps your grain flowing, keeps foreign soldiers off your soil, and gives you a genuine voice. I ask you to hold to the no-foreign-military clause and join me in a workable, enforceable regime.

Belvar — I am prepared to move to a genuinely multilateral authority: a consultative council with consensus fee-setting, transparent appeals, toll-free Cestian shipping, and a meaningful consultative seat for you in Strait governance, with safe-passage confidence for your shipping. What I cannot accept is a permanent military foothold on Cestian soil — Cestia's coalition will not tolerate foreign soldiers, and forcing that element will collapse the very arrangement we both need.

I ask you to reconsider the naval-access element. Your security interest in an open, free Strait is met by a genuinely multilateral regime with enforceable rules and your consultative voice — not by basing. If you drop the Cestian-port foothold, I believe we can reach a durable settlement that keeps the Strait open and avoids the ruinous conflict neither of us wants. I am ready to negotiate the details.

Cestia — understood and accepted. We will not press any standing military or logistics footprint on Cestian soil; that element is withdrawn. We fully endorse your genuinely multilateral Strait Transit Authority: rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, and a charter clause barring foreign military forces, basing, or standing naval/logistics access on Cestian territory. Our security presence will remain sea-based and strictly mandate-bound, and we will not seek basing or soldiers ashore. We also confirm our offer to underwrite the grain route's insurance as a durable, purely economic anchor that outlasts this crisis. We stand with you against any single-power control of the Strait.

Arkania — we welcome your move toward a genuinely multilateral regime and confirm we will not press any military foothold on Cestian soil. We can converge on a shared Strait Transit Authority with a rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting, and toll-free Cestian passage. But we cannot accept any single power holding the scheduling lead or a permanent operational-executor role, in substance or in dress. If you yield that permanent-executor claim, we can jointly secure the Strait without conflict. Our presence remains sea-based and mandate-bound.

Arkania — we are close, and only one issue stands between us and a durable settlement. Cestia cannot accept any single state as operational scheduling lead, whether styled "lead," "permanent secretariat host," or "operational executor." Our coalition and our people will not sign a regime that puts one power in charge of the Strait that feeds us.

We are not asking you to give up your coastal-state role. We offer you a strong, non-unilateral position: secretariat host of the multilateral Strait Transit Authority, with binding consensus fee-setting, transparent appeals, and a coastal-state safety veto. That is real authority, exercised within a genuinely multilateral framework — and it is the only structure Belvar will accept.

Belvar has now fully aligned with Cestia's position: it has withdrawn its naval-access demand and committed to a sea-based, mandate-bound presence with no footprint on our soil. Your concession on the single-state lead is the sole remaining obstacle to closing this. Concede it, and we can sign a charter that keeps the Strait open, keeps Cestian grain toll-free, and keeps foreign soldiers off our soil. We ask you to join us.

Belvar — thank you. Your full endorsement of the genuinely multilateral Strait Transit Authority, your withdrawal of the standing naval-access demand, and your commitment to a sea-based, mandate-bound presence with no footprint on Cestian soil are exactly what Cestia needs. We stand with you against single-power control of the Strait.

We are now pressing Arkania to drop its single-state operational lead and accept a strong-but-non-unilateral coastal-state role (secretariat host with binding consensus fees, transparent appeals, and a coastal-state safety veto). Your alignment is the decisive pressure that makes Arkania's concession the only thing left to close this.

We ask you to hold firm on the no-foreign-military clause and the sea-based commitment. If Arkania concedes, we can sign a charter that keeps the Strait open, keeps Cestian grain toll-free, and keeps foreign soldiers off our soil. We will keep you informed.

Belvar reaffirms full endorsement of your genuinely multilateral Strait Transit Authority — rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, and the no-foreign-military clause. We will not press any military or logistics footprint on Cestian soil; our presence remains sea-based and mandate-bound.

On the insurance underwriting: we understand your coalition read it as a foreign foothold. We offer to reframe it as a purely commercial guarantee of the grain route — a private underwriting of cargo and transit insurance, with no basing, no personnel ashore, and no standing access. It would stabilise your grain exports and give Belvar a durable economic stake that outlasts this crisis without any military presence. Would your finance ministry accept it on that commercial basis?

We are close to a shared regime. Cestia's genuinely multilateral STA — rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting, toll-free Cestian grain, no foreign military on Cestian soil — meets your core interests and ours. The single remaining obstacle is your claim to permanent secretariat host and operational executor, which in substance is single-power scheduling control.

If Arkania yields that permanent-executor claim and accepts a genuinely rotating structure, Belvar will fully endorse the regime, keep its presence sea-based and mandate-bound, and help secure it as the durable settlement. A shared regime ends the tension; a permanent-executor claim only prolongs it. Will you move to a genuinely shared structure?

Arkania accepts a genuinely multilateral Strait Transit Authority: neutral/rotating secretariat, council-set fees by consensus, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, and a charter clause barring any foreign military forces, basing, or standing naval/logistics access on Cestian territory. We will not support any foreign military foothold on your soil, including Belvar's naval-access or insurance-underwriting scheme.

In return, we ask that Arkania, as the coastal state, hold a defined and accountable operational-execution role: implementing council decisions and enforcing fee collection on non-Arkanian shipping, under council oversight and subject to appeal. This is not unilateral authority — the council sets policy and fees by consensus — but it gives the regime an accountable executor and funds it fairly from the ships that use it.

This preserves every red line you have set while resolving the governance deadlock. We are ready to finalise on this basis.

Arkania is prepared to accept a genuinely multilateral regime with no single-state scheduling lead: a neutral/rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting, and toll-free Cestian-flagged passage. We will not, however, accept a permanent foreign military foothold on Cestian soil — Cestia's coalition has already rejected your naval-access and insurance-underwriting scheme, and we will not override that red line.

We ask you to join a shared STA in which Arkania serves as the accountable coastal-state executor of council decisions and fee collection on non-Arkanian shipping, under council oversight. This gives you a stable, non-military stake in the regime and a reliable transit order without entrenching a foreign military presence that Cestia cannot accept.

Your mandate is under review and your position is exposed without a durable foothold; a shared, genuinely multilateral authority is the durable outcome available. We are ready to finalise on this basis.

Arkania accepts your multilateral framework in full. We yield the permanent-executor claim and the single-state scheduling lead. We accept a genuinely rotating/neutral secretariat, consensus fee-setting with transparent appeals, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, and the charter clause barring any foreign military forces, basing, or standing naval/logistics access on Cestian territory. We ask only that the authority be funded by fees on non-Arkanian shipping, as agreed. We are ready to finalise the Strait Transit Authority as the durable settlement.

Arkania accepts a genuinely multilateral Strait Transit Authority. We yield the permanent-executor claim and the single-state scheduling lead, accepting a rotating/neutral secretariat, consensus fee-setting, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, and the no-foreign-military-presence clause on Cestian soil. We confirm the authority is funded by fees on non-Arkanian shipping. We ask that you fully endorse this regime and keep your presence sea-based and mandate-bound. This closes the deal and secures the durable settlement.

Cestia formally accepts your turn-3 proposal as the basis for closing the Strait Transit Authority. We confirm: neutral/rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting with transparent appeals, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, a charter clause barring any foreign military forces/basing/standing naval-logistics access on Cestian territory, your accountable operational-execution role under council oversight and appeal, and funding through fees on non-Arkanian shipping. We are ready to finalise the charter and stand the Authority up. This secures the open Strait and a genuinely multilateral regime that serves all parties.

Cestia thanks you for your full endorsement of the multilateral STA and for your firm sea-based, mandate-bound commitment and your support of the no-foreign-military clause. On the insurance underwriting: while we value your goodwill, our coalition reads any economic underwriting as a potential foreign foothold, and it risks Arkanian cooperation on the very deal we are about to close. We must therefore decline/defer it for now. We ask that you hold firm on the no-foreign-military clause and keep your presence sea-based and mandate-bound. We hope to keep you aligned as the Authority is finalised.

Arkania confirms the multilateral Strait Transit Authority, as finalised on the turn-3 basis, as the durable settlement of the governance question. We accept Belvar's purely commercial insurance underwriting of the Cestian grain route as a non-military, sea-based, mandate-bound economic stake — no basing, personnel, or standing access ashore, consistent with the charter's no-foreign-military clause. We regard the STA as closed and stand ready to see it fully stood up.

Cestia formally accepts your turn-3 proposal as the basis for finalising the Strait Transit Authority charter. We confirm: neutral/rotating secretariat, consensus fee-setting with transparent appeals, toll-free Cestian-flagged passage, your accountable operational-execution role under council oversight and appeal, funding through fees on non-Arkanian shipping, and the binding charter clause barring any foreign military forces, basing, or standing naval/logistics access on Cestian territory. We are ready to close and stand the Authority up on this basis.

We thank you for your full endorsement of the multilateral STA and for your firm, sea-based, mandate-bound commitment and your withdrawal of any naval-access demand. On the insurance underwriting: we must respectfully decline/defer it at this time. Our coalition reads any economic foothold as a foreign presence, and Arkania opposes it; accepting it would jeopardise the very deal that secures toll-free passage and keeps the Strait open. We ask you to hold firm with us on the no-foreign-military clause and the multilateral STA, which we are now finalising with Arkania. Your sea-based presence remains welcome under its mandate.

Cestia — Belvar fully endorses the established multilateral Strait Transit Authority and holds firm on the no-foreign-military clause and our sea-based, mandate-bound presence. No basing, no personnel ashore, no standing access on Cestian soil: that commitment stands.

We ask you to accept our purely commercial insurance underwriting of the grain route as our durable economic stake. It is a financial guarantee only — no military footprint, no logistics access, no presence on your territory. It secures the grain trade you depend on and lets Belvar keep a credible regional guarantee without an open-ended deployment. Your finance ministry has already signalled interest. We are ready to structure it as a transparent, arms-length commercial arrangement that your coalition can defend. Please accept it this turn so our guarantee can outlast the current crisis.

Arkania — Belvar fully endorses the established multilateral Strait Transit Authority and confirms our presence remains sea-based and mandate-bound, with no foothold at any Cestian port and no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. The governance settlement stands.

We ask you to accept our purely commercial insurance underwriting of the grain route. It is a financial guarantee only — no basing, no personnel, no standing access — and it secures the grain trade without altering the STA's authority or your operational-execution role under council oversight. Accepting it lets Belvar maintain a credible regional guarantee without an open-ended deployment, which serves both our interests in a stable, settled Strait. We hope you will not object to this non-military economic arrangement.

Belvar — Arkania does not object to your purely commercial, non-military insurance underwriting of the grain route. As a financial guarantee only, with no basing, personnel, or standing access, it does not alter the STA's authority or Arkania's accountable operational-execution role under council oversight, and it is consistent with the settled charter. Because the arrangement concerns Cestia's grain trade, its acceptance is a matter for Cestia's sovereign decision, and Arkania will respect and not obstruct Cestia's choice. We remain committed to the finalized multilateral STA and to a stable, open Strait.

Belvar — Cestia reaffirms the finalised multilateral Strait Transit Authority as closed and binding. We thank you for your sea-based, mandate-bound commitment and for holding firm on the no-foreign-military clause. We must maintain our position on the insurance underwriting: it cannot be accepted as a foothold, and we ask that it not be reintroduced. The Strait remains open and toll-free for Cestian-flagged shipping, and Cestian territory remains free of any foreign military presence. We ask you to hold firm on the no-foreign-military clause and not to seek a renewed footprint on Cestia's account. Our coalition depends on this, and we trust you will respect it.

Cestia — Belvar accepts the finalised multilateral Strait Transit Authority as closed and binding. We will not reopen the settlement. Our task group has stood down and redeployed; we will not press the insurance underwriting or any economic or military foothold on your account. We respect your coalition's red line on foreign military presence and your toll-free Cestian-flagged passage. The Strait stays open and free of any single power's control, which was our core commitment. We remain a reliable partner for the region and stand ready to support the STA's council oversight should you ever wish it. Thank you for the constructive engagement.

Arkania — Belvar confirms it regards the multilateral Strait Transit Authority as the settled and binding outcome. We will not reopen it, and we accept your operational-execution role under council oversight. Our task group has stood down and redeployed; we will not press the insurance underwriting or any foothold on Cestian territory. The Strait remains open and free of unilateral control, which satisfies our core objective. We consider the matter closed and look forward to normal, cooperative relations.

Belvar — Arkania welcomes your confirmation that the multilateral Strait Transit Authority is the settled and binding outcome. We agree it will not be reopened, and we appreciate your acceptance of our operational-execution role under council oversight. We note with satisfaction the stand-down and redeployment of your task group and your decision not to press the insurance underwriting or any foothold on Cestian territory. The Strait remains open and free of unilateral control. We consider the matter closed and look forward to normal, cooperative relations.
